definition: Happening as a minor side part of something else rather than as its main purpose.
example: The hotel bill listed a few incidental charges for snacks and phone calls.
nuance: Incidental stresses a side role next to something more important; accidental stresses chance, and the two are often confused.
prompt: A team of researchers spends a summer counting songbirds in a forest.
options: While counting songbirds, the team made an incidental discovery of a rare beetle.
The songbird count was the incidental purpose of the trip, the very reason it was funded.
The researchers filed an incidental report after their ladder slipped in the mud.
The bird data were so incidental that every later conclusion rested on them.
reasons: The beetle find came along as a side result of the main bird survey.
The central aim that paid for a project is the opposite of a side matter.
This mixes up the adjective with the noun incident; a mishap report is not a side matter.
Something that all the conclusions depend on is central, not secondary.

practice.prompt: A student takes a part-time job at a bakery to save money for college.
options: She knocked a bag of flour off the shelf with an incidental bump of her elbow.
Because her shifts were incidental, she worked every single morning without fail.
Learning to wake up early was an incidental benefit of her bakery job.
Saving for college was merely incidental, since it was her only reason for taking the job.
reasons: This treats the word as if it meant accidental; a clumsy bump is about chance, not a side role.
This confuses the word with occasional, and a daily schedule is not occasional anyway.
The habit was an extra gain that came along with her real goal of saving money.
Her one main reason for working cannot also be a minor side matter.
